sustainable-forestry-s2.title: Wildfire in burned and unburned forest plots

table.caption: A wildfire swept through a pine forest where some plots had prescribed burns in the past 5 years and others did not (invented data for practice)
rows: Fuel on forest floor before the wildfire (metric tons per ha)

items.q: Which forestry method harvests some trees and leaves most of the forest standing?
options: Selective cutting
Clearcutting
Prescribed burning
Slash-and-burn

why.correct: Selective cutting removes chosen trees, often single mature ones, from a standing forest.
options: Right: some trees are taken, most remain.
Clearcutting removes all the trees.
Prescribed burning removes brush, not timber.
Slash-and-burn clears land for farming.

items.q: Why does selective cutting cause less erosion than clearcutting?
options: Most trees stay, so roots hold the soil
The cut trees are left on the ground to block the stream
Selective cutting is done in winter, when there is no rain
The soil under selected trees is harder, so it does not move

why.correct: Standing trees keep roots in the soil and leaves over it.
options: Right: roots and canopy remain.
Logs in streams are not the reason.
Logging season is not what limits erosion.
Soil hardness is not the reason.

items.q: How does a prescribed burn reduce the harm from later wildfires?
options: It burns brush, so later fires have less fuel
It kills the large trees, so wildfires have nothing tall to burn
It adds moisture to the soil, so the forest is unable to burn
It leaves ash that blocks oxygen from reaching future fires

why.correct: Less fuel on the ground means lower, cooler fires that large trees survive.
options: Right: less fuel, cooler fires.
Prescribed burns are planned so large trees survive.
Burning does not add moisture.
Ash does not block oxygen from later fires.

items.q: Which is a drawback of selective cutting compared with clearcutting?
options: It costs more per log to harvest
It causes more erosion because the soil is left bare
It removes more habitat for forest animals
It makes streams warmer by removing the shade over them

why.correct: Felling and hauling single trees through a standing forest takes more time and care.
options: Right: higher cost per log.
Selective cutting leaves soil covered.
It removes less habitat.
Most shade remains.

items.q: A company replaces a cut native mixed forest with a plantation of one fast-growing pine species. Compared with regrowing the native forest, which is a likely cost?
options: Lower biodiversity, as one tree species supports fewer animals
Lower wood production, because pines grow slowly
More soil erosion, because pines have no roots
More shade on streams, because pines are taller

why.correct: A single-species plantation is a monoculture with less variety of food and shelter.
options: Right: a monoculture supports fewer species.
Plantations are chosen because they grow wood fast.
Pines have roots that hold soil.
Shade is not the cost described.

items.q: Which action by a family most directly lowers the demand for cutting trees?
options: Buying recycled paper and reclaimed wood
Buying more new paper products made from fresh wood
Burning wood in a fireplace instead of using gas heat
Replacing wooden fences with new ones every two years

why.correct: Reused and recycled wood fiber replaces wood that would otherwise be cut.
options: Right: reuse and recycling replace new wood.
New paper from fresh wood raises demand.
Burning more wood raises demand.
Frequent replacement raises demand.

items.q: A 5,000-hectare forest grows 4 m³ of new wood per hectare each year. To harvest sustainably, how many cubic meters of wood can be cut each year at most?

why.correct: Yearly growth: $5{,}000\,\text{ha} \times \frac{4\,\text{m}^3}{1\,\text{ha}} = 20{,}000\,\text{m}^3$. Cutting no more than that keeps the forest from shrinking.

mistakes.why: Multiply the area by the growth per hectare so the hectares cancel.
4 m³ is the growth on one hectare. Multiply by the 5,000 hectares.

items.q: A logging company wants to harvest timber from a forested hillside above a trout stream. Propose a forestry method and explain how it protects the stream.

why.correct: A method fitted to the hillside and stream, with how it works: selective cutting with a strip of uncut trees along the stream keeps roots holding the soil and shade over the water.

solution.label: Method
options: cut selected trees and leave a strip of forest along the stream
clearcut the whole hillside down to the water
burn the hillside before logging

why.1: Clearcutting to the water bares soil and removes shade.
why.2: Burning before logging bares the soil.

mechanism.label: How it works
options: keeps roots holding the soil and shade over the stream
removes the trees that shade the stream
adds sediment to the stream bed

effect.label: Result
options: less sediment reaches the stream and the water stays cool for trout
more sediment reaches the stream
the stream warms and loses oxygen

specific.model: The company could cut selected trees and leave a strip of forest along the stream, which keeps roots holding the soil and shade over the stream. As a result less sediment reaches the stream and the water stays cool for trout.

items.q: In the reforestation panel, what is shown?
options: Rows of seedlings planted on cut land
A few mature trees cut from a standing forest
A low fire burning brush under large trees
Large trees standing with no young trees

why.correct: The middle panel shows small trees planted where trees were cut.
options: Right: seedlings planted.
That is selective cutting.
That is a prescribed burn.
The middle panel shows young trees.

items.q: In the prescribed burn panel, why do the large trees survive the fire?
options: The fire is low, below the large trees' crowns
The large trees are cut down before the fire is set
The fire is set in the treetops, away from the trunks
The large trees are sprayed with water by the fire crew

why.correct: The flames are drawn low on the forest floor, below the crowns.
options: Right: a low ground fire spares the crowns.
The trees are standing in the panel.
The flames are on the ground.
No water spraying is shown.

items.q: Which panel's practice best matches the idea of maximum sustainable yield?
options: Selective cutting, matched to the yearly growth
Prescribed burn, because it produces the most timber
Reforestation, because seedlings can be harvested in a year
Neither, because sustainable yield applies to fish and not trees

why.correct: Taking only a portion of the trees, matched to growth, keeps the forest producing year after year.
options: Right: harvest matched to growth.
Prescribed burns do not produce timber.
Seedlings take decades to reach harvest size.
Sustainable yield applies to any renewing population, including trees.

items.q: Write the setup for the percent change in fuel on the forest floor from the unburned plots to the plots with prescribed burns, then give the answer.

why.correct: $\frac{8 - 40}{40} \times 100 = -80\%$: prescribed burns removed 80% of the fuel.

mistakes.why: Divide by the starting value, 40 metric tons per ha in the unburned plots.
That is the burned plots as a percent of the unburned (20%). Percent change subtracts first.
-32 metric tons per ha is the change. Divide by 40 and multiply by 100.
20% is how much fuel was left. The percent change is -80%.

items.q: How many times higher were the flames in plots without prescribed burns than in plots with them?

mistakes.why: Put the unburned plots' flame height (12 m) on top.
Subtracting gives the difference in meters. Divide to find how many times higher.

items.q: Which conclusion is best supported by the table?
options: Less fuel led to lower flames and fewer large trees killed
More fuel on the floor led to lower flames and fewer large trees killed
Prescribed burns killed more large trees than the wildfire did
Flame height had no link to the number of large trees killed

why.correct: Burned plots: 8 metric tons of fuel, 1.2-m flames, 10% of large trees killed. Unburned: 40, 12 m, 75%.
options: Right: less fuel, lower flames, fewer deaths.
More fuel went with higher flames and more deaths.
The table shows deaths in the wildfire, lower in burned plots.
Higher flames went with more trees killed.

items.q: A town sits next to the unburned forest. What does the table suggest the town should support?
options: Prescribed burns or fuel removal near the town
Putting out each small fire, so fuel keeps building on the floor
Planting more brush near homes to block the wind
Removing the large trees and leaving the brush behind

why.correct: Reducing fuel near homes lowers flame height and spread, protecting both forest and town.
options: Right: less fuel near the town means a lower fire.
That is what built up the 40 metric tons of fuel.
Brush adds fuel.
Leaving brush and removing big trees makes fires worse.

items.q: Put the steps of a sustainable selective harvest in a sensible order.
options: Survey the forest and measure how much wood it grows each year
Mark mature trees to cut, keeping strips along streams
Cut and haul out only the marked trees
Replant or let seedlings regrow in the gaps, then monitor

why.correct: Measure growth, choose trees, harvest only those, then regrow and monitor.
